title: Beruriah and the open page
hookLine: women study Talmud today; communities differ about how
carry: beruriah read closely, and the page kept her

cards: Some rough neighbors were making Rabbi Meir's life miserable, the Talmud says, so miserable that he prayed they would die. His wife, Beruriah, stopped him. What are you basing this on?
He pointed to a verse in the Psalms: let sinners cease out of the earth. Read it again, she said. The Hebrew can be read as sins, not sinners.
Let sins cease. And look at the end of the verse: then the wicked will be no more. Pray that they turn back, and there will be no more wicked.
He did, and the Talmud says they turned back. A woman, reading closely, correcting a sage.

teach.b: The page is open. You met Beruriah and Ben Azzai last year; today, where that old argument stands now. First, Beruriah.
She appears in the Talmud by name, as a sharp reader of scripture, and her argument turns on a single word. The sages kept her reading on the page. Second, an old disagreement, kept honestly.
The Mishnah in tractate Sotah records two views. Ben Azzai says a man is obligated to teach his daughter Torah.

Rabbi Eliezer objects, and says teaching a daughter Torah is like teaching her foolishness. Both views stay in the Mishnah, side by side, and later generations had to decide which one to walk by. Third, today.

teach.h: TODAY: STUDY HALLS AND DAILY PAGES.
teach.b: Women study Talmud in classes, in study halls, with study partners and in daily page-a-day cycles, and some have celebrated finishing the whole of it.

Communities differ on this, and say so openly. Orthodox communities disagree among themselves about how and what women should study, with some building serious programs of Talmud study for women and others holding back.
Conservative, Reform and Reconstructionist movements teach Talmud to women and men alike, including in rabbinic training.
Fourth, the page itself. In Hebrew, a page of Talmud is a daf. Remember the Vilna edition: the same page everywhere.
The page doesn't check who opened it. It just asks to be read closely, the way Beruriah read.

how: Women study Talmud in women's study halls, synagogue classes, university courses and daily page cycles, alone or with a study partner. Communities differ in what they offer and encourage.

games.q: what does “the page is open” mean?
o: women studying Talmud today, as communities differ
a rule that any page may be read on Shabbat
a custom of leaving the Talmud open overnight

games.q: the page is open — tap the pairs.
p: a man must teach his daughter Torah

s: the Talmud records Beruriah correcting a sage's reading of a verse
she told Rabbi Meir to read 'sins', not 'sinners', and to pray that his neighbors turn back.
the Mishnah speaks with one voice about teaching daughters Torah
Ben Azzai says a father must; Rabbi Eliezer objects. both views are kept.
every Jewish community today agrees on women's Talmud study
communities differ, and Orthodox communities differ among themselves.

games.q: you're Beruriah. your husband, Rabbi Meir, is praying that his troublesome neighbors would die, citing a verse: let sinners cease out of the earth. what do you say?
o: pray harder; the verse supports you.
read it again: let sins cease, not sinners. pray that they turn back.
games.why: Beruriah rereads the verse, and Rabbi Meir prays for his neighbors instead. the Talmud says they turned back.

practice: Bring to mind someone who's learning something right now, a child with homework, a friend in a new job, someone who started late and feels it, and see them at their table, page open.
Find one sentence that would make them want to keep reading, not advice, just encouragement, and let it get simpler.

wordCard.voice: The page is open. Women's study of Talmud today, in communities that differ about it, and a page, a daf, that asks only to be read closely. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: a page; a leaf of the Talmud, with its two sides.

carryVoice: Your line: Beruriah read closely, and the page kept her. One close reading changed a prayer, and the Talmud is open to whoever reads that way. See you tomorrow.
